pos: n. (son of Jeconiah and father of Zerubbabel; the link in the royal line across the Babylonian captivity, called Salathiel in the New Testament)
etymology: From Hebrew She'altiel, “I have asked of God”, from sha'al, to ask, and 'El, God. The Greek of the genealogies gives Salathiel.
biblical_def: Shealtiel is a name that appears almost always in the same phrase — “Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel” — and its importance is that it carries the royal line through the ruin. His father Jeconiah was the king Jeremiah wrote off: write ye this man childless, for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David (Jer 22:30). The house of David went into Babylon under a sentence. And out of that sentenced house comes a grandson who governs Judah under Persia, rebuilds the altar and lays the temple foundation: “Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel” (Ezr 3:2). Haggai brings the word of the LORD to him by that name (Hag 1:1) and ends the book with a reversal of the curse itself: “will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the LORD, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee” (Hag 2:23) — the signet ring that Jeconiah had been plucked off and thrown away. Matthew keeps the chain intact: “Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel” (Mat 1:12). The line God cursed is the line God restored, and the man in the middle of it is Shealtiel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Shealtiel; in sacred history he is the son of Jeconiah and father of Zerubbabel, in the royal line of David.
webster_full: SHEALTIEL, n. The name signifies I have asked of God.
He was a son of Jeconiah, king of Judah, carried captive to Babylon.
His son Zerubbabel was governor of Judah under the Persian kings.
In the genealogies of Matthew and Luke the name is written Salathiel.
Through him the line of David is continued from the captivity to the birth of Christ.
scriptures: Now in the second year of their coming unto the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, began Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the remnant of their brethren the priests and the Levites, and all they that were come out of the captivity unto Jerusalem; and appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to set forward the work of the house of the LORD.

In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying,

In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the LORD, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee, saith the LORD of hosts.
And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel;
corruption_summary: The two genealogies of Christ are offered as a plain contradiction, and Jeremiah's curse on Jeconiah as a defeater of the Davidic promise; both objections dissolve once the texts are actually read.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew calls Shealtiel the son of Jechonias and Luke calls him the son of Neri, and the discrepancy is a standing exhibit against the reliability of the Gospels. The historic answers are neither novel nor strained: Matthew traces the legal succession to the throne through Joseph, Luke the natural descent through Mary; or a levirate marriage places one man in two lines; or one evangelist gives the line of inheritance and the other the line of blood. The dictionary does not insist on a single solution and does insist that an unexplained difficulty is not a demonstrated error. Two writers with access to the temple registers, writing for readers who had the same registers, would not both blunder over the most scrutinized pedigree in Israel.

The weightier objection is Jeremiah's. Jeconiah was declared childless and no man of his seed was to prosper on David's throne — yet Christ descends from him. Notice what the curse actually forbids: sitting upon the throne of David and ruling any more in Judah. No son of Jeconiah ever did; Zerubbabel was a governor under Persia, not a king. The line continued and the crown did not, until One came whose right to the throne was not by legal descent through Joseph alone but by the virgin birth — David's son by Mary, Jeconiah's heir by law, and the curse untouched. Haggai's signet oracle is the first hint of it, and Gabriel finishes the sentence: “the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David” (Luk 1:32).
roots_summary: Hebrew She'altiel (H7597), Shealtiel, I have asked of God; sha'al (H7592), to ask; chotham (H2368), signet, seal; Zerubbabel (H2216); Greek Salathiel (G4528).
roots_lines: Hebrew She'altiel (H7597) — Shealtiel; I have asked of God.
Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask, request, enquire; the first element of the name.
Hebrew chotham (H2368) — signet, seal; the emblem of authority restored to his son.
Hebrew Zerubbabel (H2216) — Zerubbabel; his son, governor of Judah and builder of the temple.
Greek Salathiel (G4528) — Salathiel; the form of the name in Matthew and Luke.
usage: “Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel” — the phrase that carries a dynasty through an exile.
“Jechonias begat Salathiel” — the cursed king begets the restored line.
“I will make thee as a signet” — the ring thrown away, taken up again.

pos: n. (the Persian chancellor whose letter halted the rebuilding of Jerusalem; also a Levite who repaired the wall under Nehemiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Rechum, connected with racham, to have compassion — “compassionate”. The chancellor of Ezra 4 bore a merciful name and wrote a merciless letter.
biblical_def: Rehum the chancellor is the official who stopped the work at Jerusalem for the better part of a generation. When the adversaries of Judah were refused a share in building the temple, they turned to the imperial post: “Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king” (Ezr 4:8). The letter is a model of its kind — professed loyalty to the crown, an appeal to the archives, and a warning that this rebellious and bad city, once rebuilt, would pay no toll, tribute or custom. The king searched the records, found that Jerusalem had indeed made insurrection of old, and ordered the work stopped. “Now when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power” (Ezr 4:23). The haste is the detail that gives them away. A second and very different Rehum appears in Nehemiah's day, a Levite with a trowel: “After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani” (Neh 3:17), and a Rehum seals the covenant of Nehemiah 10. The same name serves the opposition and the rebuilding, which is how it usually goes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Rehum; in sacred history the name belongs to the Persian chancellor who wrote against Jerusalem, and to a Levite who repaired the wall.
webster_full: REHUM, n. The name signifies compassionate or merciful.
Rehum the chancellor wrote to Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of Jerusalem.
By his letter the work of the house of God ceased until the second year of Darius.
A Levite of the same name, the son of Bani, repaired a portion of the wall under Nehemiah.
Others of the name are found among those who returned with Zerubbabel and sealed the covenant.
scriptures: Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king in this sort:

Now when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power.
After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani. Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part.

Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as it is written in the law of Moses the man of God.
corruption_summary: Opposition to the work of God is expected to come as open persecution; Ezra 4 shows it arriving as paperwork, legality and concern for public order, which is far commoner and harder to answer.
corruption_paragraphs: The adversaries in Ezra 4 begin by asking to help build. Refused, they hire counsellors, weaken the hands of the people, and finally write a letter that is accurate in most of its particulars and devastating in its effect. Nobody in the story breaks a law. The opposition is procedural, respectable and successful, and it costs the temple sixteen years. The church has generally braced for the lion and been undone by the clerk. Scripture's counsel for such seasons is not a technique but a posture: the elders of the Jews kept building when the word of God came by Haggai and Zechariah, and answered the next enquiry by telling the plain truth about who they were and whose house it was (Ezr 5:11).

There is a second lesson in the two Rehums. One used an office to stop the work; the other took a section of broken wall and repaired it. Nehemiah 3 is a chapter of names doing exactly that — goldsmiths, apothecaries, rulers of districts, a man and his daughters — and the wall went up in fifty-two days because a great many people each mended what was in front of them. The New Testament has the same architecture: the body “maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love” when “every joint supplieth” and every part works in its measure (Eph 4:16). Chancellors get letters into the archives. Levites with trowels get walls built.
roots_summary: Hebrew Rechum (H7348), Rehum; racham (H7355), to have compassion; be'el te'em, chancellor, lord of decree; saphar (H5608), scribe; batel, to cease, be made to stop.
roots_lines: Hebrew Rechum (H7348) — Rehum; the name means compassionate.
Hebrew racham (H7355) — to love deeply, have mercy; the root of the name.
Aramaic be'el te'em — lord of the decree, rendered “chancellor”; his office under Persia.
Hebrew saphar (H5608) — to write, to be a scribe; Shimshai's office beside him.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, repair; the verb of Nehemiah 3, used of the other Rehum.
usage: “Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem” — opposition with a filing number.
“They went up in haste… and made them to cease by force and power” — the eagerness gives the motive away.
“After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani” — the same name, the other side of the wall.

pos: n. (a name borne by several men of the restoration; chiefly the son of Jehiel who called Israel to repentance over the strange wives)
etymology: From Hebrew Shekanyah, “the LORD hath dwelt” or “dwelling of the LORD”, from shakan, to dwell or tabernacle, with the divine name. It is a common name in the post-exilic books.
biblical_def: Shechaniah is one of the recurring names of the return, and its most significant bearer speaks a single sentence that changes the course of Ezra's ministry. Ezra had learned that the returned people, priests and Levites among them, had married the women of the surrounding nations, and had torn his garment and sat down astonied. It was Shechaniah who broke the silence: “And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing” (Ezr 10:2). Three things are in that sentence, and they are the anatomy of true repentance: he names the sin without softening it, he says we though his own name is not on the guilty list, and he refuses despair. Other men of the name appear across the same books — a father whose sons returned with Ezra (Ezr 8:3), the keeper of the east gate's father (Neh 3:29), and a Shechaniah of Arah whose son-in-law was Tobiah the Ammonite, a marriage alliance that gave Nehemiah's enemy ears inside Judah (Neh 6:18). The book is honest about both: the same name on the side of repentance and on the side of compromise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Shechaniah; in sacred history it is the name of several men of the restoration, chiefly the son of Jehiel who moved Israel to put away the strange wives.
webster_full: SHECHANIAH, n. The name signifies the LORD hath dwelt.
Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, first confessed the trespass of the strange wives.
He counselled Ezra to make a covenant with God, and said, Arise, for this matter belongeth unto thee.
Another Shechaniah is named among the chief of the fathers who went up with Ezra.
A third, of the sons of Arah, was father in law to Tobiah the enemy of Nehemiah.
scriptures: And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing.
Of the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh; Zechariah: and with him were reckoned by genealogy of the males an hundred and fifty.
After them repaired Zadok the son of Immer over against his house. After him repaired also Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate.
For there were many in Judah sworn unto him, because he was the son in law of Shechaniah the son of Arah; and his son Johanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah.
corruption_summary: Ezra's reform is condemned as ethnic cleansing, and Shechaniah's confession as cruelty toward women and children; the text's own categories are religious, not racial, and the objection ignores what was actually at stake.
corruption_paragraphs: The putting away of the strange wives is the passage most often used to charge the Old Testament with racism, and the charge does not survive contact with the rest of the canon. The same Scripture makes Rahab of Jericho and Ruth of Moab mothers in the royal line, commands Israel to love the stranger, and provides in the law for a foreign woman taken into an Israelite house. What Ezra faced was not foreign blood but foreign gods: a remnant of a few thousand, newly returned from a captivity that had come upon them for idolatry, contracting the exact alliances that had produced it — and the priests leading the way. Nehemiah put the argument in one line: “Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things?” (Neh 13:26). The question was whether there would be a people left to receive the Messiah at all.

It should still be said plainly that this is a hard passage, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise: Ezra weeps, the people sit trembling in the rain, and the matter takes months to sort out family by family. The dictionary does not read it as a standing rule for the church — Paul explicitly forbids a believer to dismiss an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay (1Co 7:12-13) — but as an extraordinary act in a unique covenant crisis. The abiding lesson is Shechaniah's, and it is about repentance rather than divorce: name the sin as ours, refuse to explain it away, and do not conclude that it is too late. “Yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing.”
roots_summary: Hebrew Shekanyah (H7935), Shechaniah; shakan (H7931), to dwell, tabernacle; ma'al (H4603), to trespass, act treacherously; nokri (H5237), foreign, strange; miqveh (H4723), hope.
roots_lines: Hebrew Shekanyah (H7935) — Shechaniah; the LORD hath dwelt.
Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to settle, abide, dwell; the root behind the Shekinah glory.
Hebrew ma'al (H4603) — to act unfaithfully, trespass; his word for what the people had done.
Hebrew nokri (H5237) — foreign, alien; the “strange wives” of the reform.
Hebrew miqveh (H4723) — hope, expectation; “there is hope in Israel concerning this thing”.
usage: “We have trespassed against our God” — a man confessing a sin that was not on his own record.
“Yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing” — repentance that refuses despair.
“The son in law of Shechaniah the son of Arah” — the same name inside the compromise.

pos: n. (a chief Levite of the return, overseer of the temple workmen and a leader of the great confession under Nehemiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Qadmi'el, “God is the ancient one” or “before God”, from qedem, east, front, antiquity, with 'El. His house returns as one unit of seventy-four with Jeshua.
biblical_def: Kadmiel is one of the two Levitical names that anchor the whole restoration. His family comes back in the first company: “The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodaviah, seventy and four” (Ezr 2:40) — a strikingly small number, which is why the Levites who did come are named so carefully. When the foundation of the temple was laid, he was one of the overseers: “Then stood Jeshua with his sons and his brethren, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together, to set forward the workmen in the house of God” (Ezr 3:9). Nearly a century later he is still on the stairs. At the great assembly after the reading of the law, “Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God” (Neh 9:4), and it was these men who called the people to their feet with the summons that opens the longest prayer in the Old Testament: “Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise” (Neh 9:5). Foundation, confession, and the courses of thanksgiving (Neh 12:8) — the house of Kadmiel is present at all three.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Kadmiel; in sacred history he is a chief of the Levites who returned from Babylon and led in the service of the second temple.
webster_full: KADMIEL, n. A Levite, named with Jeshua at the head of the returning Levites.
The children of Jeshua and Kadmiel were seventy and four in number.
He was set with his sons over the workmen in the building of the house of God.
He stood upon the stairs with the Levites at the great confession under Nehemiah.
His name is found among the courses appointed for thanksgiving.
scriptures: The Levites: the children of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the children of Hodaviah, seventy and four.

Then stood Jeshua with his sons and his brethren, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together, to set forward the workmen in the house of God: the sons of Henadad, with their sons and their brethren the Levites.
Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
corruption_summary: The smallness of the returning remnant is treated as failure, and the long public confession of Nehemiah 9 as a relic of a guilt-driven religion; Scripture treats both as the ordinary shape of restoration.
corruption_paragraphs: Seventy-four Levites came back. Priests returned in their thousands and Levites in dozens, and the men who had the least to gain from the ruined house are the ones the record names. It is a small beginning, and the modern instinct is to measure such a work and find it wanting. Zechariah, prophesying to that generation, anticipated the instinct and forbade it: “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). The old men who had seen the first house wept when they saw the foundation of the second, and the shouting and the weeping could not be distinguished from one another — which is a fair description of most genuine revival.

The second corruption is a distaste for corporate confession. Nehemiah 9 has Israel standing a quarter of the day reading the law and a quarter confessing, and Kadmiel is one of the men leading it — a public, detailed, historical recital of national sin going back to the wilderness. A therapeutic religion cannot use such a chapter; it hears only shame. But the prayer does not end in shame. It ends in covenant, and its refrain throughout is that God is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and of great kindness, and that He did not forsake them in the wilderness. Confession that is honest about sin is the only kind that can afford to be honest about grace: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1Jn 1:9).
roots_summary: Hebrew Qadmi'el (H6934), Kadmiel; qedem (H6924), east, front, ancient time; Lewi (H3878), Levi; yasad (H3245), to found, lay a foundation; barak (H1288), to bless.
roots_lines: Hebrew Qadmi'el (H6934) — Kadmiel; God is the ancient one.
Hebrew qedem (H6924) — east, front, antiquity; the first element of the name.
Hebrew yasad (H3245) — to found, establish; the laying of the temple foundation he oversaw.
Hebrew barak (H1288) — to kneel, to bless; the summons of Neh 9:5.
Hebrew todah (H8426) — thanksgiving, confession; the Levitical course named in Neh 12:8.
usage: “The children of Jeshua and Kadmiel… seventy and four” — the whole Levitical return, counted.
“To set forward the workmen in the house of God” — the office of a man who keeps others building.
“Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever” — the call that opens the great prayer.

pos: n. (a Levite of understanding brought to Ezra at Ahava, entrusted with the temple silver, and a teacher of the law under Nehemiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Sherebyah, of uncertain derivation, ending in the divine name Yah. Ezra names him among the sons of Mahli, of the house of Levi.
biblical_def: Sherebiah enters the record at the river Ahava, where Ezra had gathered the returning company and discovered a serious defect: he “viewed the people, and the priests, and found there none of the sons of Levi”. He sent for men, and the answer to that errand is credited where Ezra always credits things: “by the good hand of our God upon us they brought us a man of understanding, of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel; and Sherebiah, with his sons and his brethren, eighteen” (Ezr 8:18). He was then given one of the most exposed jobs of the journey. Ezra had refused a military escort, having told the king that the hand of God is upon all them for good that seek Him, and so the treasure crossed the desert unguarded: “Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them” (Ezr 8:24), weighed the silver and gold into their hands, and told them they were holy unto the LORD and so were the vessels. Years later he is teaching. At the reading of the law he is among the Levites who “caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place” (Neh 8:7), and he stands on the stairs at the confession and seals the covenant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Sherebiah; in sacred history he is a Levite of the sons of Mahli, who came to Ezra at Ahava and served in the second temple.
webster_full: SHEREBIAH, n. A Levite of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi.
He came with eighteen of his sons and brethren to Ezra at the river Ahava.
He was of the twelve to whom the silver, the gold and the vessels were weighed for the journey.
He was among the Levites who caused the people to understand the law at the reading thereof.
He stood upon the stairs at the confession, and sealed the covenant with Nehemiah.
scriptures: Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them,

Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Nehemiah 8:8 is the Bible's own charter for expository preaching, and it is regularly displaced by preaching that entertains, moralizes or campaigns instead of giving the sense of the text.
corruption_paragraphs: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” is one verse and a complete theory of preaching. Read the text; read it plainly; explain what it means; keep at it until the people understand. Sherebiah and his brethren did nothing else, and the result was a national repentance and then a feast, because Nehemiah told them the joy of the LORD was their strength. Most of what displaces expository preaching in the modern pulpit fails one of those four clauses — the text is not read, or not read plainly, or the sense given is the preacher's rather than the passage's, or nobody troubles to see whether the people understood. Paul's charge to Timothy has the same four parts: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2).

The second thing worth naming is Ezra's refusal of an escort, since it is the setting of Sherebiah's commission. Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers, having boasted that God protects those who seek Him — and then he did not merely trust and hope; he weighed the treasure publicly into the hands of twelve named men and weighed it publicly out again at the other end. Faith and scrupulous accounting are not rivals. The same apostle who taught the churches to give also took care that no man should blame him in the abundance administered by him, “providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2Co 8:21).
roots_summary: Hebrew Sherebyah (H8274), Sherebiah; sakal (H7919), to be prudent, understand; qodesh (H6944), holy, set apart; shaqal (H8254), to weigh; bin (H995), to discern, cause to understand.
roots_lines: Hebrew Sherebyah (H8274) — Sherebiah; a Levite of the house of Mahli.
Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be prudent, act wisely; behind “a man of understanding” at Ahava.
Hebrew shaqal (H8254) — to weigh out; the treasure weighed into and out of his hands.
Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — holiness, that which is set apart; “ye are holy unto the LORD”.
Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, understand, cause to understand; the verb of Neh 8:7-8.
usage: “By the good hand of our God upon us they brought us a man of understanding” — Ezra's way of describing a recruitment.
“Caused the people to understand the law” — the Levite's whole business.
“Gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” — expository preaching, defined once for all.

pos: n. (a chief of the porters who kept the gates of the house of the LORD after the return; also a Levite who taught the law)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Aqqub, connected with 'aqab, to take by the heel, to follow or supplant — the same root as Jacob. Several men of the return bear it.
biblical_def: Akkub belongs to the porters, the doorkeepers of the temple, and the record is careful about them in a way that repays attention. His house comes back in the first company: the children of the porters, listed by families, “in all an hundred thirty and nine” (Ezr 2:42). The Chronicler names him among the chief of them: “And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren” (1Ch 9:17). Nehemiah counts the guard again after the wall is up — “Moreover the porters, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two” (Neh 11:19) — and lists them once more keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates (Neh 12:25). An Akkub is also among the Levites who caused the people to understand the law at Ezra's reading (Neh 8:7). Doorkeeping does not look like much until one asks what a temple with no gatekeeper becomes. These men decided daily what and who came into the house of God, kept the vessels and the chambers, and opened the doors every morning. The psalmist knew the office and coveted it: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Akkub; in sacred history he is a chief of the porters or doorkeepers of the second temple, and the name of a Levitical teacher.
webster_full: AKKUB, n. The head of a family of porters who returned from the captivity.
The porters are named with Shallum, Talmon and their brethren, keeping the gates of the house of the LORD.
They numbered an hundred seventy and two in the days of Nehemiah.
Their office was to keep the ward at the thresholds of the gates, and to open the house every morning.
A Levite of the same name assisted in causing the people to understand the law.
scriptures: The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all an hundred thirty and nine.
And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief;
Moreover the porters, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two.
Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that guarding the door of God's house is a real and honourable office, and that a church which will not guard its threshold will not keep its faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Akkub is a doorkeeper in a list of doorkeepers. What his office presses on is a modern discomfort with boundaries in the church — the sense that any threshold is exclusion and any guard a gatekeeper in the pejorative sense. Scripture takes the opposite view. The porters were Levites, an ordained order with a charge, and Nehemiah's first act after the wall was finished was to appoint the gates and the keepers, because a wall with unwatched gates is a wall in name only. The elders of a congregation hold the same office in a different form: they “watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17).

The principle to recover is that guarding is a service of love and not of suspicion. The porter opened the house every morning to whoever came to worship; his business was to keep out what defiled, not to keep out people. Paul charges the elders at Miletus in exactly those terms — feed the flock, and know that grievous wolves shall enter in among you, not sparing the flock (Act 20:28-29). A church with no doctrine of the threshold ends by admitting anything and confessing nothing. And the honour of the work is settled by the psalm: a day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere, and the doorstep of His house is better ground than the tents of the wicked.

pos: n. (a name of the restoration: a builder on the wall, a sealer of the covenant, a son of Asaph among the temple singers, and a Reubenite spy)
etymology: From Hebrew Zakkur, “mindful” or “remembered”, from zakar, to remember. Several men of the name appear, and the sense of the name suits the books that record them.
biblical_def: Zaccur is a name that turns up wherever something is being remembered or rebuilt. The earliest bearer is a Reubenite among the twelve spies, Shammua the son of Zaccur (Num 13:4), whose tribe's representative brought back the evil report. After the exile the name belongs to better men. One takes a section of Jerusalem's wall near the beginning of the work: “next unto him builded the men of Jericho. And next to them builded Zaccur the son of Imri” (Neh 3:2). Another seals Nehemiah's covenant among the Levites (Neh 10:12). A son of Asaph named Zaccur stands in the first of the twenty-four courses of temple musicians — “Of the sons of Asaph; Zaccur, and Joseph, and Nethaniah, and Asarelah… which prophesied according to the order of the king” (1Ch 25:2). And a Zaccur is remembered for something rarer than any office: his son Hanan was made an assistant treasurer of the temple stores, and Nehemiah gives the reason in five words — “for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren” (Neh 13:13). Wall, covenant, song, and an honest hand on the storehouse keys. The name means remembered, and Scripture remembered them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Zaccur; in sacred history it is the name of several men, including a builder of the wall, a Levite who sealed the covenant, and a son of Asaph.
webster_full: ZACCUR, n. The name signifies mindful, or remembered.
A Reubenite, the father of Shammua, one of the twelve sent to search the land.
The son of Imri, who builded a portion of the wall of Jerusalem next to the men of Jericho.
A Levite who sealed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah.
A son of Asaph, appointed with his brethren to prophesy with harps and cymbals in the house of the LORD.
scriptures: And next unto him builded the men of Jericho. And next to them builded Zaccur the son of Imri.
Of the sons of Asaph; Zaccur, and Joseph, and Nethaniah, and Asarelah, the sons of Asaph under the hands of Asaph, which prophesied according to the order of the king.

And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah: for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that faithfulness in unglamorous trust — a section of wall, a storeroom key, a place in a choir — is what Scripture records and rewards.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The men called Zaccur are too minor to have been contested. What the name gathers, almost by accident, is a picture of ordinary faithfulness in four departments: a length of wall built next to the men of Jericho, a signature on a covenant, a place in a course of singers, and a family trusted with the stores because they were counted faithful. None of these is a career. Each is a charge. The New Testament makes the same standard explicit for anyone holding anything on another's behalf: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

The principle to recover is the honour of the small trust, particularly where money is concerned. Nehemiah had just found the temple chambers rented out to Tobiah and the Levites gone back to their fields for lack of support, and his remedy was to appoint treasurers whose character was known. He gives no other qualification. Not ability, not lineage, not eloquence — counted faithful. Churches and ministries have been wrecked by men gifted in every respect but this one, and Scripture's warning is direct: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” (Luk 16:10).

pos: n. (a name borne by several Levites and captains: a receiver of the temple treasure under Ezra, an overseer of the outward business of the house of God, and one of David's men at Ziklag)
etymology: From Hebrew Yozabad, “the LORD hath bestowed”, a shortened form of Yehozabad, from zabad, to give or endow, with the divine name.
biblical_def: Jozabad is one of the workhorse names of the Levitical books. At Ezra's arrival in Jerusalem he is on the receiving end of the desert treasure: “on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God… and with them was Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites” (Ezr 8:33). A Jozabad stands among the Levites who caused the people to understand the law at the great reading (Neh 8:7), and another is named among those who had taken strange wives and put them away (Ezr 10:23) — the record does not spare the Levites when it lists the guilty. Under Nehemiah a Jozabad holds an office worth pausing on: “Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chief of the Levites, had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God” (Neh 11:16). Somebody had to manage the supply, the stores, the labour and the accounts, and Scripture names the men who did it. Earlier still, two men of the name are among the captains who came over to David at Ziklag, mighty men of Manasseh who helped him against the band of raiders (1Ch 12:20). The name means the LORD has given, and it is attached, over and over, to men handling what He gave.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Jozabad; in sacred history it is the name of several Levites and captains, chiefly officers of the second temple.
webster_full: JOZABAD, n. The name signifies the LORD hath bestowed.
A Levite, the son of Jeshua, who received the weighed treasure at Jerusalem with Ezra.
One of the Levites who caused the people to understand the law at the reading thereof.
A chief of the Levites who had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God.
Captains of Manasseh of this name fell to David at Ziklag, and helped him against the rovers.
scriptures: Now on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest; and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas; and with them was Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites;
Also of the Levites; Jozabad, and Shimei, and Kelaiah, (the same is Kelita,) Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.

Also Jeshua, and Bani, and Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodijah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law: and the people stood in their place.
And Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chief of the Levites, had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God.
corruption_summary: The administrative work of the church is treated as a lower order of service than the spiritual, when Scripture names the men who kept the outward business and ordained an office for it.
corruption_paragraphs: “The outward business of the house of God” is a phrase that deserves rescuing. It covers the stores, the labour, the repairs, the tithes and the accounts — and it was held by chief Levites, ordained men, whose names Nehemiah records alongside the singers and the porters. There is a persistent notion that such work is a distraction from ministry, tolerated because somebody must do it. The apostles thought otherwise. When the Grecian widows were neglected in the daily distribution, they did not treat the problem as beneath them; they created an office for it and required that the men chosen be “of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3). Character requirements that high are not set for menial work.

The second thing the name presses is the honesty of the record. A Jozabad taught the people the law; another Jozabad is on the list of Levites who had married foreign wives and had to put them away. Scripture does not clean up its Levites. The same books that record the reading of the law and the sealing of the covenant record the priests' own compromise, Eliashib's chamber let out to Tobiah, and the tithes unpaid so that the singers had gone back to their farms. A history written to flatter the clergy would look nothing like Ezra and Nehemiah. That candour is one of the quiet arguments for the truth of the whole.

pos: n. (the name of several men of the return: a priest who came up with Zerubbabel, a Levite of Merari, and men who put away strange wives and sealed the covenant)
etymology: From Hebrew Malluk, “reigning” or “counsellor”, from malak, to be king, to reign. It is a royal name carried by priests and Levites in a nation with no king.
biblical_def: Malluch appears four or five times across the restoration books and once in the Chronicler's Levitical rolls, and the pattern of the appearances is the interest. A Malluch is among the priests who came up with Zerubbabel in the first return: “Amariah, Malluch, Hattush” (Neh 12:2). A Malluch is among the sons of Bani who had taken strange wives in Ezra's day and are named in the list of those who put them away: “of the sons of Bani; Meshullam, Malluch, and Adaiah” (Ezr 10:29). And a Malluch sets his seal to Nehemiah's covenant, in which the people bound themselves with an oath to walk in God's law, not to give their daughters to the people of the land, to keep the sabbath, and not to forsake the house of their God: “Hattush, Shebaniah, Malluch” (Neh 10:4). A Malluch of the sons of Merari stands in the Levitical genealogy of the singers (1Ch 6:44). Priest, offender, covenanter, singer — whether these are one man or several, the books put the name on both sides of the same reform, which is what an honest register looks like when the men in it are sinners being restored.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Malluch; in sacred history it is the name of several priests and Levites of the return from Babylon.
webster_full: MALLUCH, n. The name signifies reigning, or counsellor.
A priest who went up with Zerubbabel in the first return from the captivity.
One of the sons of Bani, who had taken a strange wife and put her away in the days of Ezra.
One of the chief of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah.
A Levite of the sons of Merari, in the genealogy of the singers appointed by David.
scriptures: And of the sons of Bani; Meshullam, Malluch, and Adaiah, Jashub, and Sheal, and Ramoth.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
corruption_summary: Lists of bare names are skipped as filler, and the sealed covenant of Nehemiah 10 is dismissed as legalism; the first loses the doctrine of the register, the second mistakes covenant for merit.
corruption_paragraphs: A page of names with no story attached is the part of Scripture readers most reliably skip, and the habit costs something. These registers are the proof that the restoration happened to actual households in actual towns; the returning families are counted, the guilty are named, the covenanters sign. It is the same instinct that makes Luke date the Baptist's ministry by six named rulers. Christianity is a historical religion or it is nothing, and it keeps records because the events it rests on are events. Paul's argument for the resurrection is a list of witnesses, most of them still alive and available to be questioned (1Co 15:5-6).

The second correction concerns the covenant Malluch sealed. Nehemiah 10 is sometimes read as a relapse into works-religion — a people signing up to keep rules. But the chapter follows the confession of Nehemiah 9, which recites Israel's failures for thirty verses and grounds every hope in God's mercy; the covenant is the response of the pardoned, not the price of pardon. That is the order everywhere in Scripture: God redeems Israel out of Egypt and then gives the law at Sinai; Christ saves, and then commands. “If ye love me, keep my commandments” (Joh 14:15) is not a bargain. Obedience that follows grace is gratitude; obedience that hopes to purchase grace is another religion altogether.

pos: n. (a descendant of David who returned with Ezra; also a priest of the first return and a repairer of the wall)
etymology: From Hebrew Chattush, of uncertain derivation. The Chronicler places one bearer in the royal genealogy, among the sons of Shemaiah in the line of Shechaniah and Zerubbabel.
biblical_def: Hattush is a small name with a large placement. The Chronicler lists him in the royal genealogy after the exile: “the sons of Shemaiah; Hattush, and Igeal, and Bariah, and Neariah, and Shaphat, six” (1Ch 3:22) — the house of David, still being counted generations after the throne was gone. Ezra names him at the head of his own company: “Of the sons of Phinehas; Gershom: of the sons of Ithamar; Daniel: of the sons of David; Hattush” (Ezr 8:2). That is the order of the muster — two priestly houses, then the royal house, represented by one man travelling as a private citizen in a caravan of returning exiles. A Hattush repairs a section of the wall next to Jedaiah (Neh 3:10); a Hattush is among the priests who came up with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:2); and a Hattush seals the covenant (Neh 10:4). The son of David who goes up to Jerusalem in Ezra 8 has no crown, no court, and no prospect of one. He simply comes home when the way opens, and takes his place in a list. The line was being kept, in obscurity and by ordinary men, until the day the angel would say of one of them, “the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David” (Luk 1:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hattush; in sacred history he is a descendant of David who returned with Ezra, and the name of a priest and of a repairer of the wall.
webster_full: HATTUSH, n. A son of Shemaiah, in the line of David after the captivity.
He went up with Ezra from Babylon, being reckoned of the sons of David.
A priest of the name came up with Zerubbabel in the first return.
A Hattush, the son of Hashabniah, repaired a portion of the wall of Jerusalem.
One of the name sealed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah.
scriptures: And the sons of Shechaniah; Shemaiah: and the sons of Shemaiah; Hattush, and Igeal, and Bariah, and Neariah, and Shaphat, six.
Of the sons of Phinehas; Gershom: of the sons of Ithamar; Daniel: of the sons of David; Hattush.
And next unto them repaired Jedaiah the son of Harumaph, even over against his house. And next unto him repaired Hattush the son of Hashabniah.
corruption_summary: The obscurity of David's line after the exile is read as evidence that the messianic promise failed; Scripture treats the same obscurity as the promise being kept in a manner nobody would have chosen.
corruption_paragraphs: For four centuries after Zerubbabel the house of David holds no throne, and the sceptical reading concludes that the promise of an everlasting kingdom quietly lapsed. What the registers show instead is a line kept with care by men of no consequence — a Hattush in a caravan, names copied into Chronicles for a community that had no political use for them. The promise was never that David's sons would reign continuously; it was that his throne would be established for ever, and Isaiah had already described the manner: a stump, a root out of dry ground, no form nor comeliness. “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isa 11:1) — a stem is what is left when the tree has been cut down.

The second thing to draw out is how ordinary the faithfulness looks from inside. Hattush went up to Jerusalem because Ezra was going and the road was open. He is one name in one list, and he could not have known that the register he was entered in would be scrutinized by every generation of the church. That is the usual condition of obedience: a man does the next right thing without seeing what it is for. “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58).
